raw_text:
The subcutaneous implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (S-ICD) was developed to preserve the mortality benefit of ICD therapy while avoiding the intravascular and intracardiac leads that account for many acute and late complications of transvenous ICDs. Contemporary guidelines consider an S-ICD appropriate for patients with a standard ICD indication who do not require bradycardia pacing, cardiac resynchronization, or antitachycardia pacing (ATP) [29,30]. The concept was validated in early human feasibility work by Bardy and colleagues, which showed that a left lateral generator and parasternal subcutaneous electrode could reliably sense and defibrillate ventricular fibrillation without entering the heart or vasculature [1]. The pivotal IDE study subsequently demonstrated acceptable safety and efficacy, leading to regulatory adoption [2].

The evidence base has matured from feasibility cohorts to large registries and randomized comparisons. Pooled IDE and EFFORTLESS data showed high conversion efficacy and an acceptable complication profile through 2 years [3]. The U.S. post-approval study extended these findings in a broader, more comorbid population, including patients receiving dialysis, and reported high acute implant success and low perioperative complication rates [4]. One-year post-approval outcomes confirmed effective therapy for ventricular arrhythmias, although mortality reflected the underlying risk of the enrolled heart-failure population rather than device failure [5]. The EFFORTLESS registry provided important real-world data: midterm outcomes showed durable shock efficacy and manageable complication and inappropriate shock rates [6], while 5-year follow-up confirmed sustained final shock efficacy, few conversions to transvenous systems for pacing indications, and no structural lead failures in that early-generation cohort [7].

Randomized data have clarified comparative performance. PRAETORIAN randomized patients with ICD indications but no pacing requirement to S-ICD or transvenous ICD and demonstrated noninferiority for the composite of device-related complications and inappropriate shocks [8]. Subsequent analyses showed that appropriate shocks from the S-ICD were effective, whereas transvenous ICD recipients benefited from ATP for some monomorphic ventricular tachycardia episodes [9]. A secondary PRAETORIAN analysis emphasized the trade-off: fewer lead-related complications with S-ICD but different profiles of pocket, sensing, and shock-related issues [10]. ATLAS, enriched for younger patients and those at higher lead-complication risk, found fewer perioperative lead-related complications with S-ICD, with similar early defibrillation effectiveness but more implant-site pain and a nonsignificant trend toward more inappropriate shocks [11]. Observational propensity-matched data likewise suggest fewer lead-related complications with S-ICD, although patient selection and programming are critical [24].

Implant technique has evolved substantially. Early implants used a three-incision subcutaneous approach; a two-incision technique simplified electrode tunneling without apparent loss of safety [12]. In the post-approval cohort, two- and three-incision approaches had similar 3-year outcomes, with shorter procedure times for the two-incision technique [13]. Intermuscular generator placement between the serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi is increasingly favored to improve cosmesis, comfort, and defibrillation vectors [14]. Because S-ICD defibrillation depends on system geometry, the PRAETORIAN score uses chest radiographs to identify suboptimal generator or coil position and predict conversion failure [15]. Most recently, PRAETORIAN-DFT suggested that omission of defibrillation testing, guided by post-implant PRAETORIAN score assessment, can preserve first-shock efficacy while avoiding testing-related risk [16].

The principal limitation of S-ICD therapy is sensing rather than defibrillation. T-wave oversensing, myopotential noise, low R-wave amplitude, supraventricular tachycardia, and device or lead noise can cause inappropriate therapy. Preimplant surface-ECG screening reduces this risk, and ECG markers such as high T:R ratios help identify vulnerable patients [17]. Modern discrimination algorithms, dual-zone programming, and filters such as SMART Pass have lowered inappropriate shocks, as shown in contemporary observational cohorts [18] and meta-analyses [19]. The UNTOUCHED trial, enrolling primary-prevention patients with low ejection fraction and standardized contemporary programming, reported low inappropriate shock rates, supporting broader use in typical primary-prevention populations without pacing indications [20].

Patient selection remains central. The S-ICD is particularly attractive for younger patients, those with inherited arrhythmia syndromes, difficult venous access, prior device infection, dialysis, or expected long device exposure. In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, pooled registry data and single-center experience support effective therapy, although dynamic QRS/T-wave morphology and exercise-related sensing changes require careful screening and follow-up [21,22]. In children and small adults, screening failure is more common and depends on body size, ECG morphology, and lead position, but the absence of transvenous leads is compelling over decades of anticipated therapy [23]. Conversely, patients with recurrent monomorphic VT likely to be pace-terminable, symptomatic bradycardia, atrioventricular block, or need for CRT generally remain better served by a transvenous or alternative system [30].

Quality-of-life studies suggest broadly comparable psychological and functional outcomes between S-ICD and transvenous ICD recipients, though implant-site discomfort, generator size, shocks, and body image should be discussed during shared decision-making [25]. Long-term surveillance is still required: contemporary reports describe model-specific electrode advisories, extraction for infection, oversensing, or new pacing indications, and the need for individualized follow-up [26,27]. The next technological step is modular therapy: a leadless pacemaker communicating with an S-ICD has shown promising safety and device-device communication, potentially adding bradycardia pacing and ATP while preserving an extravascular defibrillation strategy [28]. Thus, the S-ICD is no longer a niche device; it is an established alternative for appropriately selected ICD candidates, with continuing refinements in implantation, screening, programming, and modular pacing likely to expand its role.
